chunks.h: What that changes for product data
chunks.t: A visitor who arrives through an assistant has usually had a set of constraints applied on their behalf before they ever see your page. They are further down the decision than organic traffic, which is a plausible reason for the conversion reversal. It also means the filtering happened somewhere you cannot see, against whatever attributes were available. If a constraint could not be evaluated against your product, your product was not in the set that got shown. There is no partial credit and no benefit of the doubt: an agent applying a filter treats a missing value as not qualifying, because that is the safe behaviour for it. A shopper might read your description and infer the screen size. An agent asked to filter on it drops you and moves on.

chunks.h: The honest limit of this argument
chunks.t: We cannot tell you what share of agent traffic you are currently losing to unrecorded attributes, and neither can anybody else, because the filtering is not observable from your side. Anyone quoting you a recovery figure for this is guessing. What is checkable is the input. You can establish which constraints buyers in your category apply, which of those your catalogue can answer, and how many of the gaps are recoverable from text you already publish. That is a measurement rather than a projection, and it is available without waiting for anything.

chunks.p: Travel filters return everything, because almost nothing is tagged
chunks.h: Travel filters return everything, because almost nothing is tagged
chunks.t: Travel Travel filters return everything, because almost nothing is tagged A traveller who needs step-free access and a cot is reading forty descriptions looking for two sentences. The facts are usually written down. They are just not fields. 31 July 2026 6 min read Travel inventory is described by people whose job is to make it sound appealing. That produces prose, and prose is the right medium for persuasion and the wrong one for comparison. The result is a results page where price and star rating are filterable because they are numbers that arrived structured, and everything a traveller actually needs to check is a paragraph.

chunks.p: Travel filters return everything, because almost nothing is tagged
chunks.t: A filter can only exclude inventory that has been tagged. Most systems, faced with untagged inventory, keep it in the results rather than dropping it, because dropping it would hide bookable stock. So a filter that almost nothing is tagged against excludes almost nothing. From the traveller's side this is indistinguishable from a broken filter, and they stop using them. Which means the one mechanism you have for helping them narrow forty options is now something they have learned to ignore. Accessibility and family requirements are the ones travellers cannot compromise on, and usually the ones nobody made filterable.

chunks.h: The cost lands after the booking
chunks.t: In retail, an unfilterable attribute costs you a sale you never see. In travel it frequently costs more than that, because the traveller books anyway and finds out on arrival. Someone who needed step-free access and got three flights of stairs generates a complaint, a refund, and a review that outlives both. The attribute would have been cheaper than any one of those.

chunks.p: Travel filters return everything, because almost nothing is tagged
chunks.h: Most of it is extraction, not acquisition
chunks.t: The encouraging part is that the facts are usually already written. "Lift to all floors" is in the description. "Cots available on request" is in the description. They are sentences rather than fields, which is exactly the case that is cheap to recover from text you already hold. Take one property set and list the constraints travellers cannot compromise on: access, family, late arrival, parking Check which of those exist as structured values rather than as sentences For the sentences, that is extraction, and it is usually the largest and cheapest share Where a fact arrives from one supplier and not another, that is mapping, which is a different cost again Whether a recovered fact is accurate enough to publish is a judgement only you can make, particularly for accessibility, where being wrong is worse than being silent. What a measurement can tell you is which absent facts are costing the most, so the verification effort goes somewhere useful.

chunks.p: Your PIM says 93% complete. Your shoppers still cannot choose.
chunks.t: Instead of asking how full the fields are, ask this: after every question your catalogue can currently answer, how many products is a shopper still choosing between? That number has a property completeness does not. It gets worse when you add products without adding facts, which is what actually happens as a range grows. And it improves only when you record something a decision turns on, which is exactly the behaviour you want from a metric that is supposed to direct work. On our test shelf, the catalogue scored 93.1% complete and still left 94 of its 216 products indistinguishable once every question it supported had been answered. Both numbers describe the same shelf. Only one of them describes the shopper's experience of it.

chunks.p: Your PIM says 93% complete. Your shoppers still cannot choose.
chunks.h: Why this is not an argument against your PIM
chunks.t: A PIM governs, enriches and distributes product information, and it does that well. Completeness is the right metric for the job a PIM is doing: it tells you whether the process is running. It was never designed to tell you whether the schema is right, and holding it to that is unfair to a tool that is doing what it was built for. Completeness is a process metric. Readiness is an outcome metric. Reporting the first and managing to the second is the mismatch. The practical consequence is that the priority list has to come from somewhere else, and then go into the PIM as work. Not instead of it.

chunks.p: Shopping ads are most of retail search spend, and your feed decides what they match
chunks.h: The expensive half is the one that looks fine
chunks.t: There are two outcomes when a high-intent query names an attribute your feed does not carry. The first is that you are not matched at all, which costs you the impression and is invisible. The second is that you get matched loosely against a broader query, and you pay for a click from somebody looking for something else. The second outcome is the problem, and campaign reporting cannot distinguish it from ordinary underperformance. It arrives as a click that did not convert. The natural response is to adjust bids and tighten negatives, neither of which touches the cause. A missing feed attribute does not look like a data problem in your reporting. It looks like a click that did not convert.

chunks.h: What the platforms say about identifiers
chunks.t: Google reports that retailers who added correct GTINs to their product data saw a 20% increase in clicks on average. Agency analyses of feed optimisation programmes report larger effects, including a roughly 70% ROAS improvement and 4.4% CTR growth in one published case, though those come from practitioners describing their own work and should be read with that in mind. The point is not the specific numbers. It is that the lever sits upstream of everything a paid media team normally controls.

chunks.p: Shopping ads are most of retail search spend, and your feed decides what they match
chunks.h: Disapprovals first, then the quiet gaps
chunks.t: Feed disapprovals and limited-performance warnings should be cleared first, because they are binary and the platform tells you about them. What the platform cannot tell you is which of the attributes it permits to be empty are the ones buyers in your category actually decide on. A feed can be fully approved, carry no warnings, and still be unable to answer the queries worth winning. Ranking the optional fields by what they would be worth, rather than by whether they are flagged, is the part nobody's dashboard does.

chunks.t: The instinct is to treat it as a front-end oversight. Somebody forgot to add the filter. Occasionally that is true, and it is a good afternoon's work when it is. More often the filter is missing because it could not be built. A filter needs a structured value on every product in the set, and what is printed on the card is frequently derived from a description rather than read from a field. The fact is visible because a template rendered a sentence. It is not filterable because there is nothing to compare. The attribute is on the page and not in the schema. A human reads it. A filter cannot.

chunks.p: 38% of ecommerce sites cannot filter on what they already show you
chunks.t: Say you accept the diagnosis and decide to fix it. Which attribute do you structure first? The usual answer is to rank by how empty each field is, because that is the number a completeness report gives you. That ranking is close to arbitrary for this purpose. A field that is 90% empty and that nobody chooses on is worth less than a field that is 40% empty and decides every purchase in the category. On a 216-product test shelf we built ourselves, ranking by absence and ranking by what shoppers said they needed disagreed completely. Processor was missing on 162 of 216 products, which put it third by absence. Only 2 of 32 stated buying requirements mentioned a processor at all, which put it last by demand. Storage and processor traded places, and fixing processor first would have been the most expensive way to change nothing. 94 of 216 products on that shelf still indistinguishable after every question the catalogue could answer our own measurement, reproducible from the repository

chunks.p: 38% of ecommerce sites cannot filter on what they already show you
chunks.h: What to do about it this quarter
chunks.t: Open your worst-performing category as a shopper, not as an admin, and try to narrow it the way a buyer would List the attributes printed on the card that you cannot filter on. That list is usually shorter and more actionable than a completeness report Rank that list by whether a purchase decision turns on it, not by how empty it is Check how much of it is recoverable from your own product titles before you budget for acquisition That last point is the one that changes project sizing. On our test shelf, storage was sitting in the product titles for 161 of 216 products, recoverable with a script. A quarter-long enrichment programme and a week of extraction look identical on a completeness dashboard and cost very different amounts.

chunks.p: 79% of product pages do not ship a full set of structured data
chunks.h: Why the product page is the hard one
chunks.t: A homepage has a handful of things on it and they are mostly navigational, so marking them up is tractable. A product page has to express everything that distinguishes one item from a near-identical one, and most of that distinguishing detail was written as prose because prose is what sells. So the richer your product copy, the larger the gap between what you have said and what a structured consumer can use. A beautifully written description is an asset to a human reader and invisible to an agent applying a filter.

chunks.p: 79% of product pages do not ship a full set of structured data
chunks.h: Structured data is downstream of recorded data
chunks.t: It is tempting to treat this as a markup task: add the schema, ship the JSON-LD, done. That works for the fields you hold. It does nothing for the fields you never recorded, and those are the ones that decide comparisons. You cannot mark up a fact you do not have. Schema coverage is capped by attribute coverage. Which puts the work in an order: find out which attributes a decision in your category actually turns on, check which of those you record, recover what is recoverable from the text you already publish, and only then argue about markup. Doing markup first produces a well-structured statement of the things you happened to have.

chunks.h: What to check on your own catalogue
chunks.t: Take one category and list the constraints a buyer would filter on. Not the fields you have, the constraints they have For each, check whether it exists as a value rather than as a sentence in the description For the ones that are sentences, that is extraction work and it is usually cheap For the ones that are absent entirely, that is acquisition, and knowing which is which before you commit is most of the value

chunks.t: Marketplaces Catalogue-wide coverage cannot tell you a seller just broke a category Onboard four thousand listings into a million-listing marketplace and coverage barely moves. The category those listings landed in can become unshoppable and nothing in the reporting says so. 14 August 2026 6 min read Averages hide distributions. That is a truism everywhere and it has a specific, expensive consequence on a marketplace. Coverage reported across the whole catalogue takes a seller who fills every field and a seller who filled three, and returns a number in the middle. Onboard a large seller whose listings are thin and the whole-catalogue figure moves by a fraction of a percent, because four thousand listings against a million is noise. The category those listings landed in is now materially worse. Coverage averaged across a million listings cannot tell you that one seller just made a category unshoppable.

chunks.p: Catalogue-wide coverage cannot tell you a seller just broke a category
chunks.h: The buyer notices before the reporting does
chunks.t: What the buyer experiences is a filter that stopped working. They narrow by material in a category that was fine last month, and now a third of the results have no material recorded. Either those listings vanish from the filtered set, which makes your inventory look thin, or the filter is quietly widened to keep them, which makes it look broken. Both teach the same lesson, which is that the filters on this marketplace are not to be trusted. This matters more here than on a single-brand catalogue because you do not control who writes the data. A retailer with a coverage problem has a process problem it can fix internally. A marketplace has thousands of independent parties each making their own decision about how much effort to spend on a listing.

chunks.p: Catalogue-wide coverage cannot tell you a seller just broke a category
chunks.t: The unit of measurement has to match the unit of the experience. A buyer does not shop your catalogue, they shop a category, so coverage has to be computed per category and attributed back to the sellers inside it. Per category, not per catalogue, because that is the set a filter operates on Attributed per seller, so an onboarding event is visible as a cause rather than as a mystery Weighted by whether a purchase in that category turns on the attribute, so effort goes to the three fields that matter rather than to every empty cell Tracked over time, because the failure mode here is a step change on a Tuesday rather than a gradual decline

chunks.p: Catalogue-wide coverage cannot tell you a seller just broke a category
chunks.t: Generic completeness nudges get ignored, and reasonably so: they treat every empty field as equally urgent, which is obviously untrue and the seller knows it. A request for three named fields, in one category, with a reason attached, is a different message and it gets acted on. Producing that message requires knowing which three, which is a ranking problem rather than a reporting one.

chunks.t: B2B Your specifications are not missing. They are in a PDF, which is the same thing. Industrial catalogues were built for buyers who know the part number. Everyone else is filtering on thread size and voltage, and those live in a supplier datasheet nobody mapped. 7 August 2026 6 min read Distribution catalogues have a particular origin that still shapes them. They were digitised from printed price lists, and a printed price list is an ordering instrument: it assumes the reader has already decided and needs the code. Search by part number works beautifully because that is the job the structure was built for. The buyer who has not decided is doing something else entirely. They have a specification to meet, and they are trying to find every part in your range that meets it.

chunks.p: Your specifications are not missing. They are in a PDF, which is the same thing.
chunks.h: Eleven parts fit and the site can show you all eleven
chunks.t: An engineer needs a valve rated to a pressure, in a thread size. Your catalogue contains eleven that qualify. The website can list them, ordered by part number, and it cannot filter by either of the two properties that decide the purchase. So they call. The sales desk answers the same specification question repeatedly and files it under service, because the catalogue was never expected to answer it. That is a reasonable thing to believe about a catalogue built from a price list, and it is no longer true about what buyers expect. The spec is not missing. It is in a PDF, which is the same as missing to everyone except the person who already knows the part number.

chunks.p: Your specifications are not missing. They are in a PDF, which is the same thing.
chunks.h: Why this sector is the cheapest to fix
chunks.t: The distinguishing fact about distribution is that the data almost always exists. It arrived with the range, in a supplier datasheet, as a table in a PDF. Nobody mapped it into a field because nobody needed it in a field while part-number search was sufficient. That makes most of the work mapping rather than acquisition, and the two differ by an order of magnitude in cost. The question worth answering before budgeting is which of your gaps are which.

chunks.p: Your specifications are not missing. They are in a PDF, which is the same thing.
chunks.t: Specification search is not a better version of part-number search. It serves a different customer: the one evaluating you against an alternative, and the one specifying a new build who has no incumbent relationship with you at all. Part-number search serves the customers you already have. Specification search is how you get the next ones, and it is also the most direct route to reducing the load on a sales desk that is currently acting as the catalogue's query interface. We will not put a number on that reduction, because we have not measured one on your traffic. The questions your desk repeats every week are a good place to point the measurement.

chunks.p: What one bit of decision information actually buys you
chunks.h: What one bit of decision information actually buys you
chunks.t: Method What one bit of decision information actually buys you A bit is one halving of the shelf. That fixed meaning is the only reason two attributes as different as screen size and processor can be compared at all. 24 July 2026 8 min read Every ranking we publish is denominated in bits, which is an unusual unit for a product data discussion and worth explaining rather than asserting. The reason is that the question is genuinely about information. A shopper facing a shelf has a set of candidates and is trying to reduce it. Every fact they learn removes some of that uncertainty. Information theory has measured exactly that since 1948, and the unit it measures it in is the bit. 1 bit means a shopper can rule out half the shelf the definition, not a scaled score

chunks.p: What one bit of decision information actually buys you
chunks.t: Completeness cannot compare unlike fields. Screen size at 60% and processor at 25% tells you which is emptier and nothing about which is worth filling. They are the same unit measuring different things. Bits are comparable because the thing being measured is the same in both cases: how much does knowing this narrow the choice? An attribute recorded on every product with an identical value scores zero, correctly, because knowing it removes nothing. An attribute recorded on nothing scores zero today and can score very highly once populated, which is the distinction that matters for planning.

chunks.p: What one bit of decision information actually buys you
chunks.t: Information alone is not enough. A field could partition the catalogue perfectly and still be worthless if no purchase decision turns on it. So each attribute is also scored against the stated requirements for the category, and a field nobody's decision depends on scores near zero however neatly it divides the shelf. This is where our ranking and a coverage ranking come apart. On our test shelf, processor was missing on 162 of 216 products, third by absence. Only 2 of 32 stated requirements mentioned a processor, which put it last by demand. Storage and processor swapped places, and that swap is the entire argument for measuring demand rather than absence. Fixing the emptiest field first would have been the most expensive way to change nothing.

chunks.p: What one bit of decision information actually buys you
chunks.t: Screen size came first in 12 of 12 runs across every seed, weighting and imputation scope we tested. Positions two through four moved between runs. We publish the whole ranking because it is informative and we say plainly that only the top of it is stable. There is also a real limitation in how we simulate a completed catalogue: we can only use values the shelf already records. Where an attribute's recorded values are unrepresentative of its true range, that simulation is wrong in a way we can name and cannot yet correct. It needs a value distribution from outside the catalogue being repaired. The measurement and the fixture it ran against are both in our repository, and one command regenerates every figure above. That is the property we would most want from a vendor making claims about our data, so it is the one we built for.

chunks.p: Why there is no conversion figure anywhere on this site
chunks.h: Why there is no conversion figure anywhere on this site
chunks.t: How we work Why there is no conversion figure anywhere on this site We have run no live experiment on merchant traffic, so we have no uplift number. Here is the experiment we would run instead, and why publishing the design is worth more than publishing a percentage. 17 July 2026 6 min read Every vendor in this category leads with a percentage. Conversion up by some amount, revenue per session up by another. We do not have one, and this is the page that explains why rather than burying it. The reason is simple and not very flattering: we have not run a live experiment on a merchant's traffic. Without one, any figure we printed would either be someone else's store or an invention. Both are worthless to you and one of them is a lie. Anyone quoting you an uplift before running a test on your traffic is quoting someone else's store.

chunks.p: Why there is no conversion figure anywhere on this site
chunks.t: The absence of a number is not the absence of a plan. This is the experiment, and we would agree it with you before it starts rather than after it finishes. Eligibility: sessions reaching a category page in the pilot category Randomisation unit: the session, stable for its lifetime Arms: the engine on, against your existing order, held back Primary metric: agreed with you before the pilot starts, not selected afterwards from whatever moved Guardrails: p95 latency, error rate, fallback rate Stopping rule: fixed in advance Reported: as a comparison against the held-back arm, including when the result is inconclusive The held-back arm is why the runtime ships with a holdback percentage on by default rather than as a setting somebody remembers to enable. A deployment without a control arm produces numbers nobody should act on, including any we would report to you.

chunks.h: What we can measure without an experiment
chunks.t: There is a whole class of claim that does not need traffic, because it is a property of your catalogue rather than of your visitors. Whether your shelf can support the decisions buyers are trying to make is measurable the day you send an export. Whether a repair improved it is measurable the week you finish. Neither of those is a revenue claim and we are careful not to let them sound like one, but both are checkable immediately and both are actionable.

chunks.p: Why there is no conversion figure anywhere on this site
chunks.t: It loses us conversations with buyers who need a vendor that already has the case studies, which is a legitimate thing to need and we would rather they find out now than in month four. What it buys is that everything else on this site can be read at face value. The figures we do publish come from a catalogue we measured ourselves, they are labelled as ours, and the command that regenerates them is on the method page. That is a smaller claim than a conversion percentage and it has the advantage of being checkable.

chunks.t: Pulse personalizes your storefront in three moves: capture anonymous in-session signals, tell us what you sell, then ask us how to order it for the visitor in front of you. The browser SDK handles the first; your backend handles the other two over a simple REST API. 1

chunks.p: API Documentation
chunks.t: Add Pulse to your website in three steps. The SDK loads in the background, so it never slows your page down, and it only reads anonymous in-session signals. No cookies, nothing personal.

chunks.p: API Documentation
chunks.t: Drop this script tag into the head of your page. It loads asynchronously and never blocks rendering. index.html Copy <!-- Add to your site's <head> --> <script src= "https://cdn.thepulseapi.com/sdk/v0/pulse.iife.js" async></script>

chunks.p: API Documentation
chunks.t: Initialize Pulse with your merchant ID and publishable key (pk_live_…). Automatic signal capture begins immediately. index.html Copy <script> window.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', () => { Pulse.init({ merchantId: 'your_merchant_id', apiKey: 'pk_live_xxx' }); }); </script>

chunks.p: API Documentation
chunks.t: Add a data-pulse-track attribute to sort dropdowns, filters, and CTAs to capture high-intent interactions automatically. product-list.html Copy <select data-pulse-track= "sort_preference" > <option value= "price_low_high" >Price: Low to High</option> <option value= "price_high_low" >Price: High to Low</option> </select> That's it, you're live : The SDK streams anonymous signals (device, referrer, scroll, clicks) to POST /v1/track and Pulse infers the visitor's persona in-session. Call the Inference API below from your backend to personalize search, recommendations, and layout.

chunks.p: API Documentation
chunks.t: You'll need a Pulse account first. Sign up to create your organization, then generate and manage your API keys from the dashboard. Sign up to get your API keys → All API requests require authentication using an API key. Include your key in the Authorization header. # Example request with authentication curl -X POST " https://api.thepulseapi.com/api/v1/session " \ -H "x-api-key: YOUR_API_KEY" Security Note : Never expose your secret API key in client-side code. All inference and catalog requests should be made from your backend servers. The browser SDK uses a publishable key (pk_live_…) scoped to event ingestion only.

chunks.p: API Documentation
chunks.t: POST /v1/session Rank a visitor session against the catalogue. Returns the ranking factors, confidence scores and the product order, with the decision record behind each one. Target latency: <50ms (p95)

chunks.p: API Documentation

chunks.p: API Documentation
chunks.t: 200 OK Copy { "persona" : { "primary" : "value_conscious_runner" , "confidence" : 0.89 , "attributes" : { "price_sensitivity" : "high" , "brand_loyalty" : "low" , "social_proof_reliance" : "high" , "purchase_intent" : "active" } }, "recommendations" : { "product_ids" : [ "prod_789" , "prod_012" , "prod_345" ], "rerank_scores" : [ 0.94 , 0.91 , 0.87 ] }, "metadata" : { "inference_time_ms" : 32 , "model_version" : "v2.3.1" } }

chunks.p: API Documentation
chunks.t: Push your products and categories to Pulse so the engine knows what it can personalize. Send a full catalog once, then keep it in sync by sending each create, update, or delete as it happens in your store. Enrichment and attribute tagging run asynchronously in the ingestion pipeline, the upsert call returns 202 Accepted immediately and the products.tagged webhook fires when a product becomes available for inference. Inference itself stays on the request path. Different credential: catalogue writes are authenticated as a signed-in dashboard session, not with the publishable pk_live_ key used for the calls above. POST /v1/products Create or update products. The call is idempotent on id , send the same product again with new fields to update it. Accepts one product or a batch. POST /v1/products Copy { "products" : [ { "id" : "prod_123" , "name" : "Performance Running Shoe" , "description" : "Lightweight cushioned trainer for daily runs" , "price" : 129.99 , "category_id" : "cat_running_shoes" , "image_url" : "https://..." , "in_stock" : true } ] } POST /v1/categories Sync your category tree so Pulse understands how products relate. Set parent_id to mirror your store's hierarchy. Upserted the same way as products. POST /v1/categories Copy { "categories" : [ { "id" : "cat_footwear" , "name" : "Footwear" , "parent_id" : null }, { "id" : "cat_running_shoes" , "name" : "Running Shoes" , "parent_id" : "cat_footwear" } ] } DELETE /v1/products/ {id} Remove a product when it is deleted or permanently out of stock. It stops appearing in recommendations immediately. Use the same pattern

chunks.p: API Documentation
chunks.t: Once the SDK is capturing signals and your catalog is synced, call these endpoints to reorder your storefront in real time for the current visitor. Call them from your backend with a Bearer token, passing the session_id the SDK created in the browser. POST /v1/catalog/ranked Return a ranked list of products personalized to the visitor's live persona, use it for "For You" grids, related products, and homepage rails. POST /v1/catalog/ranked Copy { "session_id" : "sess_abc123" , "type" : "for_you" , "limit" : 12 } 200 OK Copy { "recommendations" : { "product_ids" : [ "prod_789" , "prod_012" ], "rerank_scores" : [ 0.94 , 0.91 ] }, "persona" : { "primary" : "value_conscious_runner" , "confidence" : 0.89 }, "metadata" : { "inference_time_ms" : 28 } } POST /v1/search Re-rank your search results by intent. Send the shopper's query and Pulse orders the matching products by the persona inferred this session. Results are cursor-paginated. POST /v1/search Copy { "session_id" : "sess_abc123" , "query" : "running shoes under 100" , "filters" : [ "price:0-100" , "rating:4+" ], "limit" : 24 } 200 OK Copy { "results" : [ { "product_id" : "prod_789" , "score" : 0.94 }, { "product_id" : "prod_012" , "score" : 0.91 } ], "pagination" : { "cursor" : "eyJpZCI6IjEyMyJ9" , "has_more" : true, "limit" : 24 } }

chunks.h: Commerce has plenty of product data. It has very little decision data.

chunks.p: Teach software and AI agents what evidence a decision needs.
chunks.t: What is decision evidence? The facts a buyer needs to make a specific decision, together with where each fact came from and whether the buyer can actually see it. Product data says what is stored; decision evidence says what can be decided. Is Open Pulse the same as Pulse? No. Open Pulse is the open foundation: the SDK, the MCP server, examples, and as they are released, shared formats and category knowledge. Pulse is the paid platform that measures, prioritises, verifies and monitors, and runs the Decision API. Can AI agents use Open Pulse? Yes. The MCP server is available now: with an API key, an agent can ask which options meet a buyer's requirements and get fits, fails or cannot tell, with what is missing. Without a key, it can search our documentation. Can I use Open Pulse without the Pulse API? The SDK and the MCP server are MIT licensed and you can read, change and ship them. The decisions themselves come from the Pulse API, which needs a key. Planned formats and category packs will be usable on their own. Does Open Pulse generate missing product information? No. It never invents unverified facts. Missing dimensions, materials, compatibility, certifications or warranty terms stay unresolved until a trustworthy source provides them. Is Open Pulse a PIM? No. A PIM stores product information. Open Pulse is about the link between buying requirements and the evidence that resolves them, so it complements a PIM. What is a category pack? chunks.p: Recommendations that work on a first visit
chunks.t: How is this different from collaborative filtering? Collaborative filtering answers what people like this person bought, which needs a history and an identity. This answers what this visit implies, which needs neither. On a returning logged-in customer with years of history, a good collaborative filter has information we do not. On an anonymous first visit, it has none and we still work. Does it need a cookie or a login? No. It infers from views, searches, filters and cart actions inside the current session. Nothing is written against a person, there is no cross-site identifier, and there is no profile to export or delete because none is kept. Where can strips be placed? Any slot on any surface: product detail, cart, category and home are the common ones. The engine is asked for n ranked products and does not know or care what the placement is called. Is this a different model from your search ranking? No, and that is deliberate. It is the same ranker with the same factors pointed at a slot instead of a result set. One thing to understand, one thing to audit, and no second model quietly drifting away from the first. What happens if it is unavailable? Browsing, searching and filtering in this session are enough to move the ranking, which is also why it works on a first visit when a profile-based system has nothing to go on. How do we know it is doing anything? The held-back arm. A share of your traffic always sees your original ordering, stable per session, so the two arms can be compared on your own traffic rather than against a number we quote you. chunks.h: Half of what your catalogue records, the photograph already said
chunks.t: Visual evidence Half of what your catalogue records, the photograph already said We ran our own catalogue through the question we ask merchants, and got back an answer we did not want. Here it is, with the working. Measured in October 2026. Nothing on this page is for sale.

chunks.p: Half of what your catalogue records, the photograph already said
chunks.h: Why did we go looking for this?
chunks.t: Because of something a colleague said about their own shopping, which is the kind of remark that is unremarkable until you notice it contradicts your product. Most of the time, they said, they look at the pictures. They want to search by picture. They do not read the description. Every number Pulse produces assumes the opposite. We rank a missing field by how much recording it would narrow the shelf, and we count that field as working the moment it exists. We never asked whether anyone reads it. A fact the buyer cannot see does not decide a purchase, and we had been counting those facts at full value. So we measured it. Twice.

chunks.p: Half of what your catalogue records, the photograph already said
chunks.h: On a laptop shelf, the two channels miss each other completely
chunks.t: These are the nine things a laptop buyer weighs, typed by hand from the filter rails and buying guides of three large electronics retailers. For each one we asked two questions: can the catalogue tell you, and can the photograph tell you. Nine laptop buying facets, by whether the catalogue records them and whether a product photograph shows them What the buyer weighs Catalogue carries it Photograph shows it Memory Yes No Storage Yes No Screen size Yes No Processor Yes No Price No No Weight No No Graphics No No Battery life No No Operating system No Yes Catalogue carries 4 of 9 Photograph shows 1 of 9 Both channels 0 of 9 Nothing overlaps. Every fact we can rank on is invisible in the picture, and the one fact the picture carries is the one the catalogue never records. We expected the two channels to back each other up. They do not even meet. Honest caveat: the catalogue column is measured, the photograph column is our judgement. Screen size is the one we would argue about, and calling it visible does not change the shape of the result.

chunks.p: Half of what your catalogue records, the photograph already said
chunks.h: Then we checked our own catalogue, and it was worse
chunks.t: 2,176 products in the catalogue we use for our own demonstrations. We counted coverage per attribute, left out ratings and sales counts because those describe the listing rather than the product, and asked of each one whether a single product photograph already answers it. Colour 100.0% photo shows it Size 45.2% no Capacity 21.3% no Storage 12.9% no Memory 7.2% no Variant 3.5% no The only attribute recorded on every single product is the only one the photograph already answers. Recorded values the photo repeats 52.6% Recorded values that add something 47.4% Facts per product you cannot get by looking 0.90 Over half of everything this catalogue records is a second copy of what the picture shows. The average product carries less than one fact a shopper cannot get by looking at it. And every product has exactly one image. Not a median of one. All 2,176.

chunks.p: Half of what your catalogue records, the photograph already said
chunks.h: What does this change about the audit?
chunks.t: It adds a question we were not asking, and it turns out to be the one with the money in it. A shopper can be told a fact in three ways: a field they can filter on, a picture they can look at, or a sentence they will actually read. The audit measures the first one. So the right question is not whether an attribute is recorded. It is whether the shopper can perceive it at all, and then what the cheapest repair is. That last part matters, because the cheapest repair is often not the one we currently recommend. Today the audit says record this attribute. Quite often the attribute is already recorded and the real repair is to put it on the picture, or into the comparison table, or into the first line of the description where someone will read it.

chunks.p: Half of what your catalogue records, the photograph already said
chunks.t: Somebody has to go and get it. This is the audit we already sell, and it is the half of the problem we know how to price.

chunks.h: Generate the product showing a fact
chunks.t: A weave, a finish, a feature that nobody ever photographed. Never. This is inventing a product claim, and a picture is believed more readily than a sentence, which makes it worse rather than better. The merchant who ships it is the one who finds out. We may generate presentation. We must never generate an unverified product fact.

chunks.p: Half of what your catalogue records, the photograph already said
chunks.h: What this does not prove yet
chunks.t: It proves the overlap, because the overlap is a property of the catalogue and we counted it. It does not prove anyone loses a sale over it. The evidence for that would be a shopper opening a picture, opening it again, and leaving. We do not collect that, which is an uncomfortable thing to admit halfway down a page arguing it matters. So this is a measurement and a hypothesis, kept apart on purpose. Two things would kill it. Reordering a product gallery turns out not to change what people buy. Or merchants take the suggested photograph, shoot it, and nothing moves. We would rather find either of those out early, and we will publish it here when we do. Measured in October 2026. Nothing on this page is for sale. What we can and cannot claim is the rest of it.

If a figure cannot be reproduced, it is not printed, and that rule is why there is no uplift claim anywhere here. Start with a shelf of products and a set of questions shoppers are trying to answer. For each attribute, we compute how much recording it everywhere would improve a shopper's ability to tell those products apart, and subtract what it already contributes today. The difference is the gap, measured in bits. Bits are the right unit because the question is genuinely about information: how much uncertainty does knowing this field remove?
